name: Linear periodization

card.summary: A training plan that raises load and lowers repetitions in planned stages, used to organise progressive strength and muscle gain.

quick.overview:
Linear periodization organises resistance training into phases in which intensity (weight) gradually rises while volume falls, for example moving from higher reps to heavier, lower-rep sets over weeks. It is the traditional model behind many strength programs.

For looks, it is one way to structure progressive overload so muscle and strength gains continue, which builds the physique.
quick.how: Lifters follow blocks of weeks with a defined focus, progressing weights as the blocks advance, and sometimes a lighter week or transition phase. T Nation logs show people applying it to strongman and general training.
quick.risks: The main risks are those of weight training generally, such as strain from poor technique or overloading. Training-log posters also mention that the body does not progress in fixed linear patterns.

lead: Linear periodization is a model of training in which the programme moves through sequential phases, generally increasing load while decreasing volume as the cycle progresses. A lifter might start a block with higher-repetition sets at moderate weights and move over several weeks to heavier, lower-repetition work. It descends from periodization frameworks developed by Leo Matveyev around 1964 and expanded by Tudor Bompa, according to Wikipedia [1].

For appearance, it is a way of organising progressive overload, the mechanism through which muscle is built: planned increases in load keep the stimulus rising so strength and muscle size keep growing, which changes physique. Progressive overload itself is traced to Thomas DeLorme's 1944 rehabilitation work with injured soldiers and, in legend, to Milo of Croton adding to a calf's weight daily [12].

Meta-analyses comparing linear with daily undulating periodisation have found similar hypertrophy effects [2][3], and comparisons of periodised with non-periodised training have reported advantages for maximal strength [2][9][10]. Lifters discuss linear schemes on forums such as T Nation in training logs [4][5][6].

angle.text: The plan structures progressive overload across weeks, which supports muscle and strength gains that change physique. Lifters use it to schedule heavier work and keep progress organised.

paras: Wikipedia describes the traditional framework as macrocycles, mesocycles and microcycles, with sequential blocks, for example endurance before speed and strength before power [1]. A macrocycle is a full season or annual plan, a mesocycle is a block of several weeks emphasising the same adaptations, and a microcycle is typically about a week [1]. In the classic linear form for lifting, the early block uses higher volume at lower intensity and later blocks move toward heavier, lower-rep sets, sometimes ending with a peak, a lighter week or a transition phase [1][4].

Alternatives include daily undulating periodization, where the rep range and load change from session to session within the week, and block periodization, where training is concentrated in focused blocks. Reviews often compare the linear and undulating forms directly [2][3][8].

Wikipedia traces periodization to Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome of the 1950s and the fitness-fatigue model formalised by Banister and colleagues in 1975 [1]. Leo Matveyev is regarded as one of the first to demonstrate a formalised model around 1964, after analysing Soviet Olympic athletes from 1952 and 1956, and his plans spread across the Eastern Bloc; Tudor Bompa expanded and organised the model [1]. Garhammer published one of the first US articles on periodizing strength training in 1979, and a Soviet defector shared periodization information with American strength coaches in 1988, according to the article [1].

A related lineage is progressive overload. Physician Thomas DeLorme developed progressive resistance exercise in 1944 while rehabilitating soldiers after World War II, and the principle holds that adaptation stalls unless stress keeps increasing [12]. In the popular lifting scene, novice linear progressions, in which the load rises session after session, are associated with Mark Rippetoe and Lon Kilgore's book Starting Strength, first published in 2005 [13].

The rationale in the periodization literature is that planned changes in load and volume let the body adapt, recover and express strength while avoiding overtraining [1][12]. Wikipedia notes that neuromuscular adaptations come first and raise strength, with muscle growth and stronger connective tissue following if the stress continues to rise [12]. Linear plans attempt to build a base with volume first and then convert it to heavier loads.

A 2017 meta-analysis of 13 studies found no meaningful difference in hypertrophy between linear and daily undulating periodisation (d = -0.02) [3]. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 studies with volume equated found periodised training improved maximal strength more than non-periodised training (effect size 0.31) but did not differ for hypertrophy (0.13, not significant); undulating beat linear for one-rep max (0.31), an effect confined to trained participants (0.61) and absent in untrained ones (0.06), with no hypertrophy difference (0.05) [2]. Earlier meta-analyses reported moderate advantages for periodised over non-periodised training for maximal strength, with effect sizes of 0.43 across 18 studies in 2017 and 0.84 in a 2004 analysis [9][10]. A 2015 meta-analysis of 17 studies (510 participants) found no difference between linear and undulating models for upper- or lower-body strength [11]. A 2026 meta-analysis of 29 studies reported comparable effects on athletic capacity and body composition, with undulating better for lean mass in people with obesity and linear suited to long-term weight loss [8].
Critics cited by Wikipedia argue that evidence for sequential blocks is thin, that the models are oversimplified and that they overlook individual variation in hormones, genetics and motivation [1].

T Nation log posters describe using linear periodisation for strongman events and linear weekly progressions [4][5], while another asks about non-linear alternatives [6]. Beginner programmes that add weight each session are the most common form lifters meet, with block-structured plans more typical of strength athletes [4][13].

A 2025 randomised trial of 22 men after ACL reconstruction found block-structured linear periodisation produced larger knee-extensor strength gains than a 3x10 programme (51% vs 26%), with a higher limb symmetry index at six months (97% vs 85%) and psychological readiness scores of 68 versus 53, while knee-flexor strength and hop performance did not differ significantly [7]. Meta-analyses in healthy lifters are described above [2][3][8][9][10][11].

timeline.event: Thomas DeLorme develops progressive resistance exercise while rehabilitating soldiers [12].
Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome becomes the theoretical root of periodization [1].
Leo Matveyev is described as demonstrating a formalised periodization model [1].
Banister and colleagues formalise the fitness-fatigue model [1].
Garhammer publishes one of the first US articles on periodizing strength training [1].
A meta-analysis finds periodised training outperforming non-periodised programmes for strength and power [10].
Starting Strength: Basic Barbell Training is first published [13].
A meta-analysis of 17 studies finds no strength difference between linear and undulating models [11].
Meta-analyses report moderate periodization benefits for maximal strength and similar hypertrophy for linear and undulating models [3][9].
A 35-study meta-analysis compares periodised and non-periodised training with volume equated [2].
A randomised trial compares linear periodisation with 3x10 after ACL reconstruction [7].
A meta-analysis of 29 studies compares linear and undulating periodization for athletic capacity and health outcomes [8].

lore.intro: Linear periodization appears in lifting forums mostly in training logs, as a scheme for organising heavier work over weeks and a point of comparison with non-linear programming [4][5][6].

claims.claim: Linear periodization builds more muscle than random training.
claims.believers: Lifters who follow planned progressions report steady gains and use the structure to schedule heavier work [4][5].
claims.experts: With volume equated, a 2022 meta-analysis found periodised training did not differ from non-periodised training for hypertrophy [2].

claims.claim: Linear periodization builds more strength than non-periodised training.
claims.believers: Posters describe linear weekly progressions as the way they add weight to the bar [4][5].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report moderate advantages for periodised programmes for maximal strength [2][9][10].

claims.claim: Undulating training is better than linear.
claims.believers: Some lifters ask about non-linear alternatives when linear progress stalls [6].
claims.experts: Hypertrophy was similar in a 2017 meta-analysis [3]; a 2022 meta-analysis favoured undulating for one-rep max in trained participants only [2]; a 2015 analysis found no strength difference [11].

claims.claim: Sequencing blocks (volume first, then intensity) is necessary.
claims.believers: Strength athletes plan volume and peaking blocks in order [4].
claims.experts: Critics cited by Wikipedia argue evidence for sequential blocks is thin [1].

claims.claim: The body does not progress in fixed linear patterns.
claims.believers: Posters note that progress stalls and use alternative plans [6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes criticism that periodization models are oversimplified and ignore individual variation [1].

claims.believers: Rehabilitation programmes use staged loading to return strength.
claims.experts: A 2025 trial after ACL reconstruction found larger knee-extensor strength gains than 3x10 [7].
